storm.summary_layperson: A storm cell near 38 dBZ is tracking about 45 miles to the WNW, but it's currently moving away from the cove and no watches or warnings are active — the broader region does carry a slight risk of severe storms through this evening, and the Sound's usual protective buffer is already thin, so a fresh cell developing closer in would find little standing in its way.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The air–water gap is already down to 4°F at 4 PM (below the 5°F threshold this framework treats as a meaningful buffer) and the trend projects it going negative by evening as air cools faster than the Sound — there's no real marine-layer protection standing by tonight.
storm.detail_html:
KOKX radar shows one tracked cell, 45 miles WNW of the cove at 38 dBZ, and it's currently moving away (closing speed −9.9 kt) — nothing is inbound toward Greenwich right now. No NWS watches, warnings, or advisories are active. Instability sits at a moderate 1,260 J/kg (HRRR f01), with unusually strong 0–6 km shear at 43 kt from the WNW. That combination is more about organization potential than immediate threat: the OKX Area Forecast Discussion notes a Slight Risk for severe thunderstorms today, with SPC mesoanalysis showing 1,000–3,000 J/kg SBCAPE building in the warm sector, and flags the limiting factor as "the amount of instability into this eve, as well as sufficient triggers."

The Sound's usual defense — a cool marine layer that chokes incoming storms as they cross the water — isn't much of a factor tonight. The air–water gap is only 4.0°F right now (water 74.8°F, air 78.8°F), already below the 5°F threshold this framework requires for a meaningful buffer, and the hour-by-hour projection has it crossing negative by around 7 PM as the air cools faster than the Sound can follow. So even though this evening's setup nominally favors Sound deflection on paper (a WNW approach, moderate CAPE that's easy to choke, slower storm motion at 11 kt), there's no standing buffer left to do that job — hence a neutral call rather than mitigating.

Net call for the window: moderate regional risk because a cell at or above 35 dBZ is within 50 miles, even though that specific cell is drifting away rather than closing. The AFD also mentions a front working through the area and a possible MCS passing through Wednesday night — worth noting because the HRRR wind forecast for this same window (see the wind section) shows a sharp jump in speed and a shift toward NE right around 7 PM, consistent with some kind of boundary swinging through later this evening, even if it doesn't organize into anything that reaches the cove.

What would change this call: a new cell developing closer than 45 miles and tracking toward the cove rather than away from it, CAPE building further toward the 1,500–3,000 J/kg punch-through range mentioned in the AFD, or the evening's apparent frontal boundary spawning fresh convection along its leading edge.

wind.tactics_blurb: RYC now: SE 126° at 2 kt, gusting 4 — light gradient wind, no sea breeze in play (deltaT only 4.0°F, just under the 5°F gate). Stays light and shifty out of the E–ENE for the first two hours, then a boundary swings through around 7 PM, nearly doubling the speed and backing hard to NNE before settling into a steadier 10–14 kt out of the NE for the rest of the window. Favor the center of the course early while it's light and wandering; once the NE fills in, pressure should even out across the cove. Expect a slow start — the real breeze doesn't arrive until the second half.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
DeltaT is only 4.0°F right now, below the 5°F gate this framework requires for a thermal sea breeze, and the coastal station network backs that up — only 5% of coastal stations are reading southerly, essentially no sea-breeze signal building. That makes today a gradient-only day, not a sea-breeze day. The authoritative airport-network gradient reads 6.0 kt, which puts it in the light bucket: raceable but thin, and prone to direction wander (this framework's flag for exactly that is a low `direction_agreement`, and tonight's is 0.52 across 29 stations — confirmation the regional wind field itself is unsettled, not just a cove-specific quirk).

RYC right now reads SE 126° at 2.1 kt (10-min avg 2.1, gusting 3.8) — close in direction to the western-LIS ensemble median (ESE 121°) but noticeably lighter than the network's 6.0 kt authoritative gradient. HRRR's own forecast direction for this hour (E 94°) diverges 32° from that live SE reading; since today isn't a Regime A/A+ sea-breeze day, the maturation correction that normally reconciles HRRR-vs-obs divergence doesn't apply, so treat the early hourly-table directions as a model estimate rather than a confirmed read — trust RYC for what's actually happening at the line right now.

The forecast table shows something more interesting than typical light-gradient drift: around 7 PM local, HRRR has speed nearly doubling (6–14 kt) with a hard back from ENE to NNE, then settling NE by 8 PM. That's a classic persistent/frontal-style shift, not thermal oscillation — there's no sea breeze here to oscillate. It lines up with the OKX AFD's mention of a front working through the area and increasing instability into this evening. It doesn't look like the classic backdoor cold-front pattern this framework watches for (deltaT is already below the 5°F ingredient-one gate, and the KBOS/KPVD/KGON sentinels are reading ESE/E/ENE rather than the NE flip that signature needs) — more likely just a synoptic trough or weak front passing through than a true backdoor.

Once the boundary clears, NE is the cleanest direction this cove sees — laminar, steady, and even across the course per the cove geography table, with maybe slightly more pressure mid-cove than tight against either shore. HRRR data runs out after 9 PM (f07–f12 failed to fetch this run), so the 10 PM row continues the settling NE trend by extrapolation rather than raw model output — treat the back half of the table as a somewhat softer call.

In racing terms: the first hour or two sits in drifter-to-light range (6–7 kt easing to 6 kt) — fine for patient light-air sailors, frustrating for anyone else. Once the boundary passes around 7 PM, conditions jump into the 10–14 kt powered-up range with gusts near 18 kt, solid one-design racing. Favor the center of the course through the transition — with direction wandering E–ENE–NNE–NE, neither shore holds a reliable edge until the NE settles in. Don't rig expecting an easy drift the whole time; the second half of the window sails noticeably harder than the first.

data_caveats: HRRR forecast wind data available only through 9:00 PM local (f01–f06); f07–f12 fetch/parse failed, so the 10:00 PM wind figure is extrapolated from the trend, not raw model output.
Ensemble direction agreement is low (0.52) across the 29-station network tonight — the regional wind field itself is unsettled, so cove direction reads carry more uncertainty than usual.

HRRR's forecast direction (E, 94°) diverges 32° from the current live RYC/ensemble reading (SE–ESE, ~121–126°); since this isn't a sea-breeze day the maturation correction doesn't apply, so early hourly-table directions may run more easterly than what's felt on the water in the next hour.
